questions.question: What does 'highest dollar amount live event' mean, precisely?
questions.known: Kalshi returns three different dollar/volume quantities per market: volume_fp (contracts traded), volume_24h_fp (contracts traded in 24h), open_interest_fp (contracts held), and notional_value_dollars, which the OpenAPI schema defines as 'the total value of a single contract at settlement in dollars'.
questions.unknown: Which of these the owner wants ranked. They are not interchangeable: notional_value_dollars is a per-contract settlement value, so it is identical across many markets and useless as a size ranking.
questions.answer_if_forced: Rank by dollars traded = volume_fp x last_price_dollars, and label it an estimate.
questions.decision_needed: Confirm the ranking metric, or accept the labelled estimate.

questions.question: Which Kalshi series belong to Gas Prices, Elections, Culture, Crypto and Golf?
questions.known: Series carry ticker, title, category and a categories list; GET /series supports a category filter that matches any entry in categories (exact, case-sensitive). The official fee schedule lists per-series tickers, which confirms a series exists.
questions.unknown: Kalshi publishes no canonical 'Gas Prices' / 'Culture' / 'Golf' category list in the API docs. The category strings used by the exchange were not enumerable from this sandbox in a documented way.
questions.answer_if_forced: Use only series tickers confirmed in the official fee schedule (KXAAAGASM; KXELECTIRAN; KXEMMY* + KXBALLONDOR; KXBTCMAX150, KXBTCY, KXETHY; KXPGATOUR, KXPGARYDER, KXPGASOLHEIM) and treat everything else as a flagged keyword match.
questions.decision_needed: Approve the seed list, or supply the exact category strings your account sees.

questions.question: How can the demo portfolio be tracked if the demo account does not exist yet?
questions.known: Kalshi's help centre states a demo account is created by signing up at demo.kalshi.co/sign-up and that it has no preloaded funds; funds are added with test payment methods. API keys are then generated in Account Settings. Demo and production credentials are not shared.
questions.unknown: Whether an account already exists for this project, and, if so, its API key ID and private key. Neither was provided and neither can be created without a human signup.
questions.answer_if_forced: Do not invent a balance. Run the browser-side paper ledger, clearly labelled, and ship a working executor that goes live the moment keys are supplied.
questions.decision_needed: A human signs up and supplies KALSHI_KEY_ID + private key path (as env vars or Actions secrets). This is the single unavoidable manual step; it cannot be delegated to an agent.

questions.question: Can the browser get true sub-second or WebSocket live prices?
questions.known: Every WebSocket session requires a signed API key at the handshake, including for public channels. REST market reads are cached for several seconds. Candlesticks only support 1, 60 and 1440 minute intervals.
questions.unknown: Nothing technical. This is settled by the docs: no anonymous WebSocket, and no sub-minute historical candles.
questions.answer_if_forced: Seconds-resolution charts must be built by accumulating REST observations; that is what the collector does. True tick-level streaming requires keys plus a server-side relay (a browser cannot hold the private key safely).
questions.decision_needed: Accept accumulated REST points, or add a key-holding relay later.

questions.question: How should a market that resolves to 'scalar' be reported?
questions.known: Market.result is an enum of 'yes', 'no', 'scalar' or the empty string. Binary markets settle at $1 per winning contract; scalar markets can settle at intermediate values.
questions.unknown: Which of the tracked five-category series are scalar rather than binary.
questions.answer_if_forced: Display the literal value returned by the API and never coerce it to yes or no.
questions.decision_needed: Say whether scalar resolutions should be counted as wins, losses or excluded in any win-rate calculation.

questions.question: What does a trade actually cost after fees, and is that modelled?
questions.known: General markets charge a taker fee of ceil(M x 0.07 x C x P x (1-P)) and a maker fee of ceil(M x 0.0175 x C x P x (1-P)). Per-series multipliers vary and some series are 0/0. There is no settlement fee and no membership fee.
questions.unknown: The fee_type and fee_multiplier actually attached to each tracked series at runtime, and the owner's membership tier.
questions.answer_if_forced: Show gross P&L and label fees as not modelled in the paper ledger; read fee_type per series from GET /series before claiming net P&L.
questions.decision_needed: Approve modelling fees at the general 0.07 / 0.0175 rates as a stated assumption, or fund a real demo account so fees come from actual fills.

questions.question: Which polling cadence is affordable?
questions.known: Authenticated requests cost 10 tokens by default against Read/Write buckets; unauthenticated public requests are limited separately; 429 returns too_many_requests with X-RateLimit-* headers and no Retry-After. GET /portfolio/balance has its own bucket (1/s or 5/s depending on tier).
questions.unknown: The account's tier, so the token budget is unknown. endpoint_costs was not queried because that needs credentials.
questions.answer_if_forced: Keep public reads modest: one collector run about every 15 minutes while the relay runs (each page shows the snapshot age), reading markets in bulk, plus four orderbooks per category, is far inside any documented limit.
questions.decision_needed: Once keys exist, call GET /account/endpoint_costs and record the tier here.

questions.question: Which site tree is canonical after five parallel sessions?
questions.known: Main contains a root-level site, a docs/ site, and two Pages mechanisms (branch deploy of / and a workflow that uploads docs/). Two mechanisms mean the deployed content can flip without a visible code change.
questions.unknown: Which tree the owner wants to keep. Both contain overlapping pages.
questions.answer_if_forced: docs/ is canonical, deployed by workflow artifact; root-level duplicates are removed.
questions.decision_needed: This session made that call (see Flagged F-05) because a single canonical tree is required for a link-checked build. Reversible from git history.

questions.question: Should the paper rules S3 and S4 be judged on the experimental high-ROI screen before an owner ROI model exists?
questions.known: S3 and S4 use the archive field high_roi, which is the dashboard's experimental 'Model watch' screen (F-14). It is a project screen, not an owner-approved model. The archive does not yet store quotes at alert time, so no S3 or S4 fill exists (F-19).
questions.unknown: Which ROI model, if any, the owner wants. Whether the screen should be the signal for any strategy at all.
questions.answer_if_forced: No. Treat S3 and S4 as exploratory. Report them with the same fee, settlement and sample-size rules as S1 and S2, and make no ROI claim.
questions.decision_needed: Owner. The simulator stays unchanged until the owner answers.

suggestions.suggestion: Make a single canonical site tree and a build step that fails on a broken link.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: Five overlapping pages with different numbers is the biggest source of wrong decisions right now. One tree means every screenshot you compare is the same site.
suggestions.risk: Removes duplicate pages other sessions created; recoverable from git history.
suggestions.success_metric: scripts/check_site.py exits 0 on every push; no 404 in the deployed site.

suggestions.suggestion: Keep a scheduled, key-free collector as the only source of live numbers on the page.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: A static page that fetches live data in your browser shows a different picture to every viewer and cannot be audited. A committed snapshot carries one timestamp and one query URL you can re-run.
suggestions.risk: GitHub scheduled workflows can be delayed or skipped; the site must therefore show the snapshot age prominently.
suggestions.success_metric: data/live/markets.json collected_at is never older than 60 minutes during market hours.

suggestions.suggestion: Show category membership basis (seed vs keyword) next to every row.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: A wrong category silently changes which 'top event' you act on. Labelling the basis lets you dismiss a heuristic match without re-deriving it.
suggestions.risk: None; it is a label.
suggestions.success_metric: Every row shows seed or keyword; the flagged count is visible on the verification page.

suggestions.suggestion: Add orderbook depth and implied ask to the ranking table, not just price.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: 'Highest dollar' is meaningless if there are 5 contracts at the touch. Contracts available at the best price decides whether a trade is even fillable.
suggestions.risk: Depth is a point-in-time read and can be stale by the time you act.
suggestions.success_metric: Every top row shows contracts at best bid and best ask.

suggestions.suggestion: Model fees before trusting any P&L number.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: Near 50 cents the taker fee is about 2 cents per contract, i.e. about 4% of a 50c stake. A strategy that looks break-even gross is a loser net.
suggestions.risk: Fee multipliers vary per series; a naive flat model misstates cost for 0/0 series.
suggestions.success_metric: Fee-adjusted P&L shown alongside gross, with the series fee_multiplier displayed.
suggestions.status: implemented (server + browser paper ledgers apply official per-series multipliers; F-84)

suggestions.suggestion: Log which chart window and which snapshot you looked at when you place each trade.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: Without that, a post-mortem cannot tell a bad rule from a bad look. It is the cheapest way to make strategy reviews honest.
suggestions.risk: Extra friction per trade.
suggestions.success_metric: Every paper trade row carries snapshot timestamp and chart window.

suggestions.suggestion: Run a resolved-market backtest before any live demo order.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: The collector already stores settled markets with their literal result. That is a free out-of-sample test set for the four proposed strategies.
suggestions.risk: Survivorship bias: markets settled before the historical cutoff are only reachable through /historical endpoints.
suggestions.success_metric: Win rate and fee-adjusted expectancy per strategy, reported with sample size.

suggestions.suggestion: Add a server-side, key-holding relay only if tick-level data is truly needed.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: It is the only way to reach WebSocket data, but it introduces key custody risk that a static site does not have. Decide it deliberately, not by accident.
suggestions.risk: Private key on a server; demo keys are lower risk than production keys but still a secret.
suggestions.success_metric: Tick latency under 1s with no key material in the repository or the browser.

suggestions.suggestion: Store the bid and ask at each alert time in the alert archive.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: It is the only way to fill a paper trade on a market that has since closed, and it gives the dashboard the quote behind each swing.
suggestions.risk: Adds two fields to an append-only archive. Existing entries stay unchanged; old entries stay unfilled.
suggestions.success_metric: Every new archive entry has a stored to_yes_bid and to_yes_ask.
suggestions.status: implemented 2026-11-20 (request R-2): scripts/build_alerts.py now stores to_yes_bid / to_yes_ask from the observation at to_time on every NEW archive entry; entries written before that are unchanged (append-only) and stay unfilled unless price_history still holds their quote.

suggestions.suggestion: Keep price history for closed markets until they finalize.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: It lets the page show the price path for a swing whose market has closed and lets the simulator mark its positions.
suggestions.risk: File size grows. Keep it bounded and keep the 120-point cap per market.
suggestions.success_metric: Every archived alert resolves to a stored observation at its to_time.

suggestions.suggestion: SHIPPED: in-browser live polling of the demo API with a CORS self-test and automatic snapshot fallback.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: Prices on the dashboard tick in near-real time (default 10s poll, 5s minimum) instead of only when the collector commits. The page says plainly which layer each number came from.
suggestions.risk: Unauthenticated request limits are undocumented; the engine polls conservatively and backs off exponentially on 429.
suggestions.success_metric: Live chip shows connected ticks; charts update within one poll interval.

suggestions.suggestion: SHIPPED: two scrolling alert chats (all events + model picks) for swings >= $0.10 in both directions.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: The alert stream is the site's pulse: every >= $0.10 move lands in the All Events chat, and model-scored candidates land in the Model Picks chat with their score reasons and modeled ROI.
suggestions.risk: Alert quality depends on poll interval; documented cache lag means faster polling cannot add information.
suggestions.success_metric: Alerts appear within one poll interval of the move; every alert carries API + book + news-lead links.

suggestions.suggestion: SHIPPED: auto-sim engine that opens/closes paper trades on 3 disclosed strategies and categorises performance by strategy, topic and price band.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: The brief asks for automated simulated trades to test strategies and categorise results. trading.html runs the loop automatically: entries on qualifying swings, exits at +/- $0.10 or settlement, and per-strategy/topic/band/exit-reason tables.
suggestions.risk: Paper fills at quoted sizes may overstate real fills; fee multipliers per series are not modelled (G5).
suggestions.success_metric: Strategy leaderboard with resolved trades and net-of-fees ROI per strategy.

suggestions.suggestion: Toast + optional sound notification when a Model Picks alert fires.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: A trader watching another tab should not miss a model pick. Toasts need no permissions; sound must stay opt-in.
suggestions.risk: Noise; keep to model picks only, off by default.
suggestions.success_metric: A pick while unfocused surfaces within 1s.

suggestions.suggestion: WebSocket market/orderbook streaming once demo API keys exist.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: REST responses are cached and can lag by seconds; the docs say to use WebSockets when you need current state. WS needs a key (F-31), so this stays blocked on credentials.
suggestions.risk: Key in the browser; demo keys only.
suggestions.success_metric: Order book refresh < 1s without extra REST load.

suggestions.suggestion: Watchlist pinning and one-click 'chart this alert' deep links between the alert chats and the dashboard.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: A trader reacting to an alert wants the price chart and book in one click, with the alert marker on the chart. Dashboard already marks swings for the selected market; extend it to deep-link from each chat bubble.
suggestions.risk: None beyond URL plumbing.
suggestions.success_metric: Alert -> chart in one click with the marker visible.

suggestions.suggestion: Add 1/60/1440-minute candlestick charts from GET /markets/{ticker}/candlesticks once the collector accumulates history.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: Seconds-resolution history cannot be requested from Kalshi; candlesticks support 1, 60 and 1440-minute intervals only. Today's chart is one-observation-per-collector-run; once enough runs exist, candlesticks add OHLC structure for free.
suggestions.risk: Rate budget for historical queries on the collector.
suggestions.success_metric: OHLC view toggles per market without breaking the seconds view.

suggestions.suggestion: SHIPPED: a second, complementary paper experiment on portfolio.html §4 — a deterministic S1–S4 strategy replay over the collected price history (entries at observed asks, exits at observed bids, official fee formula, strategy × category ledger, equity curve, settlement against the literal API result). Distinct from the alerts-page auto-sim, which trades the live alert stream.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: Tests the strategy page's stated rules against collected history with no manual input, and shows real thin-book exit slippage that a live alert trader would face.
suggestions.risk: Replay fills only at collected observation timestamps; per-series fee multipliers not applied; demo prices only.
suggestions.success_metric: Replay is deterministic per snapshot; every fill timestamp is a collected observation; fees match ceil(0.07×C×P×(1−P)) to the cent.

suggestions.suggestion: Add a candle-derived backstop feed for swings the 15-minute (relay) observation gap misses
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: F-70 shows a real 8.1c intraday move (KXPGATOUR-THRC26-MPEN, 2026-11-21) that the observation-only rule did not raise, because both surrounding snapshots read 0.00. A backstop that polls GET /series/{s}/markets/{t}/candlesticks at 1-minute resolution for the markets on the watch list would catch moves that open and close between collector runs — which is the case the brief's 'sudden swings' wording is actually about.
suggestions.effort: Medium: one more browser-side loop using the endpoint assets/live.js already wraps, plus a distinct 'candle-derived' badge so a reader can tell which rule fired.
suggestions.risk: Candles are aggregated, so a single 10c high-low range inside one minute is not the same evidence as two observed prints 10c apart. Mixing them without labelling would overstate conviction — the badge and a separate feed are what keep it honest. Rate limits apply per IP; unauthenticated requests have separate limits (https://docs.kalshi.com/getting_started/rate_limits).
suggestions.success_metric: Every alert carries its basis ('observation' or 'candle'), and replaying the F-70 case produces a candle-derived alert while leaving the observation feed unchanged.

suggestions.suggestion: SHIPPED: a pointer readout on the dashboard chart — hover reports the nearest PLOTTED contract price, its UTC time, the period's contract volume and the bid/ask when that point came from an official candle.
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: The chart was a bitmap: a trader could see a move but could not read a number off it. Reading the exact plotted value (never an interpolated one) is what turns the graph into an input to a decision, and naming whether a point is an official candle or a collector observation keeps the two commensurable.
suggestions.risk: None to the data: it reads window.__chart, which drawChart() fills with exactly what it drew. Points are matched by timestamp, so a candle and an observation at the same second report the candle's volume.
suggestions.success_metric: Hovering a plotted point prints its price, time and period volume; the number equals the plotted series' value at that timestamp (no averaging between neighbours).

suggestions.suggestion: Rank and filter the alert chats by contracts actually traded, and show the traded/quote-only ratio as a headline number instead of burying it in prose
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: On the 2026-11-21T23:01:10Z snapshot only 11 of the 48 served swings traded at or above the 100-contract floor, 19 traded below it and 13 are candle-sourced, so a trader reading the raw chat spends most of their attention on prints nobody could have executed. Sorting the chat by contracts traded (with the >= $0.10 rule unchanged) puts the executable swings first without hiding anything, and the ratio tells the reader at a glance whether today is a thin day (F-75).
suggestions.effort: Shipped in T66 as the per-row evidence chip, the published counts.evidence ratio and the 'traded only' filter; sorting the chat by contracts traded is the remaining step
suggestions.risk: A floor is a judgement call and could hide a genuine move in a thin market; mitigated by never deleting a row (the filter states how many it hid) and by printing the exact contract count on every row so a reader can apply their own threshold.
suggestions.success_metric: Within one week, the share of archived swings whose state is traded_ge_floor is visible on the page and either rises or is explained; no swing disappears without the hidden count being printed.

suggestions.suggestion: Make the alert chats something you can leave open: an opt-in sound and a browser notification for each new swing ≥ $0.10, with a per-topic switch and a mute that remembers itself
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: The brief asks for a live alerting system a person can watch in real time. A chat only alerts someone who is looking at it; a tab in the background does not. A single short tone plus a desktop notification (no text typed by the user, no account, no key) turns the page into something that can actually interrupt a trader, and the per-topic switch stops gas-price noise from drowning a golf position. It must be opt-in because browsers require a user gesture for audio and because an alert that fires on every thin print is worse than none — which is why it should be paired with the existing 'traded only' chip rather than replacing it.
suggestions.effort: Small: one toggle in the alerts toolbar, one AudioContext beep, the Notification API with a permission prompt. No build step, no dependency, consistent with the rest of the site.
suggestions.risk: Alert fatigue and false urgency: the demo exchange prints swings with zero contracts traded, so a naive sound would train the reader to ignore it. Mitigate by defaulting to off, by gating the notification on the evidence chip the reader chooses, and by never sounding for a quote-only row unless 'all alerts' is explicitly selected.
suggestions.success_metric: The toggle is exercised in the jsdom suite (off by default, one sound per alert, none on a sub-threshold move), and the page states the chosen gate in the chat header so nobody has to remember it.

suggestions.suggestion: Publish a per-topic swing-quality scoreboard (traded vs thin vs quote-only, and resolved direction) so a topic can be chosen on evidence rather than on headline size
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: The brief asks for events to stay separated by topic and for the dashboard to help a trader decide. Size alone is a poor guide: a large Culture event can print dozens of untradeable 30c swings while a small golf market prints a handful of traded ones. A compact scoreboard next to each category link would let a reader pick the topic where the prints are executable and, as alerts settle, where the direction of the move has actually matched the outcome. It is the same evidence layer already computed for the chats, aggregated rather than hidden in prose.
suggestions.effort: Medium: aggregate data/live/alerts.json counts.evidence and the alert lifecycle by category_id; render one small table on categories.html. No new data collection.
suggestions.risk: A per-topic 'accuracy' column on a sample of a few demo markets would look far more authoritative than it is. Mitigate by showing counts with the sample size attached, never a percentage alone, and by labelling any direction statistic as descriptive until the sample is large enough to be published with an interval (F-87).
suggestions.success_metric: The scoreboard renders on every category page from committed data only, its numbers reconcile with the alert page to the row, and a reader can see the sample size next to every rate.

suggestions.suggestion: Show each published row's own series record (official categories, tags, scope) with a link to it, so a topic mismatch is visible on the page instead of only in the collector
suggestions.why_it_helps_decisions: F-97 is the argument: the exchange files a natural-gas series under "Entertainment", and the site published it inside Culture until a collector rule caught it. A trader reading the Culture page cannot see WHY a row is there - the row carries a basis badge (seed / keyword / official) but not the record that decided it. Rendering the deciding record next to the row (categories, tags, scope, and the GET /series link) makes every classification auditable in one click, and turns the basis badge from a label into evidence. It is the difference between a dashboard you trust and a dashboard you check.
suggestions.effort: Low: the snapshot already carries series_categories per row and the full series_index; render them in a collapsed details cell on the category pages and the dashboard table, with the official series link. No new collection.
suggestions.risk: Too much text on a table that is meant to be scannable. Mitigate by keeping the record behind a collapsed row, showing the one decisive field by default, and never hiding the topic badge itself. A second risk is that the record is read as an endorsement of the row: the copy must say it is the exchange's own classification of the SERIES, and that the topic on this project is a decision made on top of it.
suggestions.success_metric: Every published row on every topic page can be opened to the exact GET /series record that classified it, and the class of mismatch F-97 represents is visible on the page without opening the collector.

flagged.item: The release gate never evaluated nine assertions in scripts/tests/test_scope.py: the suite printed OK and exited 0 before they ran, and three of them were false at the time
flagged.why: The file ended its checks at line ~283 with `if errors: FAIL/exit` followed by `print("OK: scope tests passed …")`. The F-72 block added later sits BELOW that report, so it executed after the summary and its findings could never affect the exit code. verify_release.py runs this file and treats exit 0 as a pass, so the gate reported 21 pages green while the dead checks were demanding fields the collector does not publish: '"open_published_rows"' and '"settled_published_rows"' in scripts/collect.py (absent), '"settled_in_scope_total_method"' (absent), and settled_in_scope_total_method in index.html (absent). Proven by running the file (prints OK, exit 0) and grepping collect.py for the strings it requires. This is a test-integrity failure, not a data failure: the page numbers it was supposed to protect were also wrong (S-02).
flagged.action: Report block moved to the end of scripts/tests/test_scope.py, so every check now gates the run. The three false assertions were made true rather than deleted: scripts/collect.py publishes counts.open_in_scope_total, open_published_rows, settled_published_rows and settled_in_scope_total_method, and index.html renders the method. Mutation-tested: removing open_in_scope_total from categories.html now makes the suite print FAIL and exit 1 (before the fix it printed OK). Re-run with `python3 scripts/tests/test_scope.py`.

flagged.item: Two pages labelled the PUBLISHED (trimmed) row count as the number of markets found in scope: categories.html for open markets, index.html for settled markets
flagged.why: scripts/collect.py computes counts.open_in_scope AFTER the per-topic keep window, so the value is the published row count (470 open rows in the 2026-11-22T06:17:12Z snapshot), while the scan had classified 12,163 open in-scope markets (470 published + 11,693 recorded in open_rows_trimmed_for_size). categories.html printed that same 470 twice: once as 'Open markets inside the five categories' and once, correctly, as 'Open rows published'. index.html did the same on the settled side: counts.settled_in_scope is the 1,600-row retained paging window, but the resolution tracker called it 'settled markets in scope' while counts.settled_in_scope_total held the scan total (6,927) and only 200 rows are published. The in-scope total for open markets was not published anywhere, so no page could have shown it.
flagged.action: scripts/collect.py now publishes open_in_scope_total (before trimming), open_published_rows, settled_published_rows and settled_in_scope_total_method (the settled paging window + historical backfill rows, with the safety-cap state). categories.html shows the scan total, the published count and the trimmed count as three separate rows; index.html names the scan total, prints the method, and labels its table 'settled rows published'. Both pages fall back to the old fields when reading an older snapshot, and scripts/tests/test_scope.py (now a live gate, S-01) fails if either label regresses. Values quoted are from data/live/markets.json collected 2026-11-22T06:17:12Z. 'High ROI' on the page means modeled ROI if the position resolves in favor at the quoted ask — a conditional figure, not an expected return.

flagged.why: Settlement pays $1 to the winning side for simple yes/no determinations, but some markets settle to a scalar value, and settlement bounds can pay partial amounts before settlement. flagged.item: The desk scan's order-book fetch returned zero books on the demo environment (both scans on main) — CAUSE NOW VERIFIED AND FIXED: the multi-market query used the wrong list encoding
flagged.why: data/live/roi.json from the desk runs committed at 2026-11-20T19:15:11Z and 2026-11-20T19:30:16Z both record counts.orderbooks = 0 for all 214 in-scope markets (3 chunks of up to 100 tickers per the documented maximum), yet scripts/collect.py's small order-book requests (4 tickers) returned 17 valid books in the 19:30:14Z snapshot the same hour, and GET /exchange/status reports the exchange active. The scan is built to degrade: it falls back to the market-level yes_bid_size_fp / yes_ask_size_fp sizes, marks depth as unknown in the reasons, and still writes a validated scan. The exact chunk failure mode was left unobserved at the time (Actions logs cannot be downloaded from a build sandbox) — Actions logs cannot be downloaded from this build sandbox (blocked host), so the cause (rate limit, chunk-size rejection, or transient demo-side behaviour) is left unverified rather than guessed.. VERIFIED SINCE, against the live demo API rather than by inference: GET /markets/orderbooks declares `tickers` as a repeated string[] (1-100 elements, 200-char maximum each), unlike GET /markets, which takes a comma-separated list. Both callers comma-joined the list, and because a ticker the API does not recognise is answered with HTTP 200 and EMPTY yes_dollars/no_dollars arrays instead of an error (documented), the request looked like a success that found no liquidity. Measured 2026-11-20: ?tickers=KXAAAGASM-26DEC31-3.30%2CKXBTCY-27JAN0100-B47500 -> one entry whose ticker is the literal joined string with both arrays empty; ?tickers=KXAAAGASM-26DEC31-3.30&tickers=KXBTCY-27JAN0100-B47500 -> both books. Not a rate limit, not a chunk-size rejection, not transient demo behaviour: a query-form mismatch, in the scan AND in the browser's live depth ladder.

Guarded by scripts/tests/test_roi_scan_snapshot.py (query form + coverage + unrequested-ticker drop) and by scripts/tests/test_pages_dom.js (the browser must never send the comma form); both were mutation-checked by re-introducing the old encoding. flagged.why: Mitigating F-40, the first version of the last step in collect.yml queued the next collection unconditionally with workflow_dispatch (documented to always create a run when called with GITHUB_TOKEN). flagged.action: Contained, then replaced. The workflow was disabled on the default branch (state disabled_manually) and the in-flight run cancelled; the run list then stayed flat, verified over several minutes. The step is now a bounded watchdog: it reads data/live/markets.json and dispatches at most one run only if the snapshot is older than 35 minutes AND nothing is queued or in flight AND fewer than 3 dispatches happened in the last hour; every branch logs its decision. Guards exercised locally in three constructed states, and a live run afterwards did not chain. Recorded on the coordination board; re-enabling on main after merge is an explicit follow-up. Measurement (2026-11-21T20:45Z, session arena-d60d648c): between this fix's merge (2026-11-21T06:49Z) and 2026-11-21T20:45Z the bounded watchdog produced ZERO dispatches; the run list in that window contains only the scheduled runs quoted in F-40 and manual workflow_dispatch runs from active sessions' branches. The watchdog did not re-chain, and it structurally cannot bootstrap a run: it executes as the last step of a collect run against a snapshot that run may have just refreshed, so a repo with no collect runs at all gets no watchdog help. Keep it (capped, harmless) but do not count it as a cadence fix. A relay cycle began on main at 21:15:08Z (run 44950553883, in progress at the time of this edit). Relay behaviour is covered by scripts/tests/test_collect_relay.py (69/69 offline per its author, mutation-tested); it is NOT yet proven over a full 5.5 h cycle on main — treat the relay like any new mechanism and re-read the run list before relying on it.

Hardened: the two workflow jobs whose concurrency groups had no time bound now have one — desk.yml scan timeout-minutes 25 (measured 4.5 min typical, 12 m 19 s slowest) and freshness-alarm.yml check timeout-minutes 10 (measured 8 s) — so a wedged runner can no longer pin those single-run groups for the full 6-hour default. collect.yml already carried timeout-minutes 350. Residual: a stalled relay can still hold the collect group for up to ~5.8 h by design; the documented remedy is cancelling the run, which restarts the chain immediately. Independently of the stall, code inspection of the same path found a second failure mode and it was fixed: scripts/collect.py's get() retried only HTTP 429 and broke the loop on the first attempt for every other status, so a single transient 5xx or a dropped connection aborted the entire pass (exit 2, nothing committed). get() now retries 429/500/502/503/504 and network errors with 1.5 s / 3 s / 4.5 s spacing over at most 4 attempts, still raises afterwards so nothing is ever written from a failed read, and still fails immediately on 400/401/403/404/410 because retrying a documented client error cannot help. Pinned by the new offline suite scripts/tests/test_collect_retry.py (6 cases), which the release gate picks up automatically because it runs every scripts/tests/test_*.py. The 429 case was then given its own schedule — 3 s, 6 s, 12 s (doubling) instead of the linear 1.5 s / 3 s / 4.5 s used for 5xx, because Kalshi's rate-limit page tells unauthenticated clients to 'back off on 429' and a collector that pages ~60 requests per pass would otherwise retry straight back into the same limit; paginated scans also pause PAGE_PAUSE_SECONDS (0.15 s) between pages to lower the odds of tripping it at all. Both are pinned in scripts/tests/test_collect_retry.py (8 cases).

flagged.item: The freshness monitor stayed silent during the collector stall because it treated any in-flight collect.yml run as healthy — a wedged run is exactly that state
flagged.why: The monitor's rescue step skipped on `if [ "$in_flight" -gt 0 ]`, so a run that was holding the concurrency group without committing looked identical to a healthy one. Measured 2026-11-22: schedule run 44970894475 held `collect-refs/heads/main` from 02:46:23Z while the newest collector commit stayed f364db9 (06:17:13Z); `data/live/markets.json` sat at collected_at 2026-11-22T06:17:12Z for ~2 h 15 m, the monitor ran and reported 'a collection is already running; not dispatching', and the chain only moved again when a human ran `gh run cancel`. The site's own banner was honest about the age throughout, so nothing false was published — the defect is that the automatic rescue could not fire in the one scenario it exists for.
flagged.action: Fixed by moving the decision into scripts/freshness_guard.py (unit-tested offline, 11 cases) and using it from .github/workflows/freshness-alarm.yml: a stale snapshot with an in-flight collector younger than 60 min (four missed passes on the relay's 15-minute grid) is left alone, because a slow pass is not a wedged one; a stale snapshot with an in-flight collector 60 min or older cancels that oldest run, and the run already pending behind it in the concurrency group starts a fresh pass from the current remote head; with nothing in flight it dispatches exactly one run, still limited to one dispatch per hour (the F-63 runaway guard). Cancelling is safe by construction: scripts/collect_relay.py re-syncs to the remote head at the top of every pass and pushes are atomic, so a cancelled pass cannot leave a half-written snapshot. The monitor is itself on the same `schedule` mechanism, so this reduces — but cannot remove — the exposure recorded in F-67/F-85.

The failing step's own output existed only in stdout. Actions job logs are served from `productionresultssa6.blob.core.windows.net`, which this project's sandbox cannot reach (`gh api .../actions/jobs/<id>/logs` returns an EOF from that host, and `gh run view --log` refuses while a run is in progress), and a run that is cancelled or times out takes its output with it. flagged.action: Fixed in scripts/collect_relay.py: every non-committing pass now calls `record_health()`, which writes `data/live/collector_health.json` — pass number, outcome, detail, at most 2,000 characters of the failing step's own output, and the run identity — and commits that file alone (never a snapshot). It returns a status instead of raising, because a diagnostic must not become a second failure, and it is idempotent when nothing changed. Pinned offline by scripts/tests/test_collect_health.py (5 cases: field shape and tail bound, only the health file is staged, no-change is not committed, a rejected push still leaves the file, and every failure path in `make_pass` routes through it). The site is unchanged by this: the landing page already states the snapshot age and the missing intervals, which is what a reader sees.

flagged.action: Fixed in scripts/collect_relay.py: the health file is now the outcome of the MOST RECENT pass in both directions. A pass that commits writes {"outcome": "ok", "detail": "snapshot committed", "snapshot_collected_at": <the snapshot it was written with>} before the commit, so it lands in the same commit as the snapshot it describes - no extra commit, no extra push, no race with the relay's own history - and a failing pass still writes "failed" and commits that file alone as before. flagged.item: The per-ticker price-history window silently deleted the observations that BOUND an archived swing, so most swings the page serves could no longer be quantified
flagged.why: scripts/collect.py keeps at most PRICE_HISTORY_LIMIT = 120 observations per ticker so the committed file stays small, and it trimmed the series to the newest 120 without regard for what the alert archive cites. The two observations that bound a swing are the ones that matter: the archive (data/live/alerts_archive.json, written by scripts/build_alerts.py) names them as from_time and to_time, and the evidence layer (scripts/alert_evidence.py) needs both to say how many contracts traded in the interval and whether the book actually repriced. Measured on the committed snapshot collected 2026-11-25T13:16:43Z: of the 150 archived swings, 62 had lost BOTH bounds and 2 had lost one - every cited ticker was still present, but the specific observations were gone. That is why the published evidence counts read traded_ge_floor 12, traded_below_floor 61, candle_unquantified 5 and unknown_no_observations 52: 52 of the 130 swings the alert chats serve could not be quantified at all, and the dashboard chart for those tickers no longer contains the swing the alert points at.
flagged.action: Fixed in scripts/collect.py. The archive is now read as the authority on which observations matter, and the observations an alert cites are PINNED: keep_observations() keeps the newest PRICE_HISTORY_LIMIT observations plus any observation whose timestamp an archived alert cites, in time order, so the chart and the evidence layer can still read the swing back. pinned_alert_times() reads from_time and to_time from data/live/alerts_archive.json and returns nothing (never a guess) when that file is missing or unreadable. The cap still bounds the file: only the observations an alert actually cites are kept in addition to the window. Pinned offline by scripts/tests/test_price_history_retention.py (8 cases: the window unchanged without pins, a pinned observation surviving the cap, an unpinned one still dropping out, the series staying in time order, a real append keeping the pin, both bounds pinned from the archive, and an absent or unreadable archive pinning nothing). The 62 swings already lost are not restored by this: a settled market is never returned by GET /markets again, and its candles are per-period closes, so the historical rows stay as they are - the fix stops the bleeding for every swing archived from now on. Verified live on 2026-11-25: after the fix, 5 observations that an archived alert cites sit outside the newest-120 window and are still present in data/live/price_history.json - they are present only because the pin keeps them, and the pass at 13:52:21Z deleted 0 cited observations. The other 129 cited observations are absent because they were deleted before the fix landed; Kalshi's GET /markets no longer returns those settled markets and its candles are per-period closes, so they cannot be re-read and are not restored by this change.

flagged.item: The browser paper simulator stopped polling before settlement and could record a provisional result as a payout
flagged.why: Kalshi distinguishes closed, determined, disputed, amended and finalized; only finalization confirms payment. The prior poll loop dropped closed and determined records, while the portfolio could book a result before finalization. It also charged a simulated taker fee on a binary payout and treated an explicit null price as zero.
flagged.action: The poll loop continues to query watched markets before finalization and includes open paper holdings even after they leave the ranked list. A lifecycle record need not contain a price, and only a finalized binary result closes a position with zero exit fee. An absent record still does not establish an outcome. Independently verified a finalized NO sample against the official demo API. Regression tests cover the lifecycle states and distinguish a missing price from zero.

flagged.item: NO-side paper exits and unrealized marks could use the wrong side of the spread
flagged.why: One minus the YES bid is a NO ask, not a NO bid. The previous simulator also accepted the last trade as an exit quote. Either can overstate a simulated strategy’s performance without any executable exit quote.
flagged.action: The browser simulator now takes price exits only on active markets, at the held side’s bid, with the documented complement of the YES ask as the NO bid fallback. Blank and non-tradable quotes do not produce marks or fills. Existing saved trades are not recalculated; new exits are tagged exit_rules_version=2 in the export. Quotes are not proof of fill size or actual fills.

flagged.item: Dashboard liquidity panel printed NO-bid prices as if they were YES asks, in reverse order - the opposite of the number a trader needs
flagged.why: Kalshi's order-book endpoint returns BIDS ONLY and the docs define the mapping explicitly: best YES ask = $1.00 - (highest price in no_dollars), and the number of contracts a buyer can lift at that ask is the count at that same no_dollars level (https://docs.kalshi.com/getting_started/orderbook_responses). dashboard.html rendered the no_bid rows themselves, reversed, under the heading 'YES asks, implied - contracts a buyer can lift'. On the committed snapshot's KXPGATOUR-MAST27-MFIT book (no_dollars [[0.973,6172.83],[0.974,6410.25],[0.975,6666.66]], confirmed field for field against GET /markets/KXPGATOUR-MAST27-MFIT/orderbook on 2026-11-27) the panel advertised 6,666 contracts at $0.975 and put the true best ask last, when the answer is 6,666.66 contracts at $0.025. The header line above it (best YES ask 2.5c) was right, so the two halves of the same panel disagreed. The brief asks for 'current liquidity amounts, how many contracts are available at a given price', which is exactly the question this column answered wrongly.
flagged.action: Fixed in dashboard.html: the ask ladder is now derived (price = 1 - no_bid price, count = that no_bid level's count) and sorted best (cheapest) first; the bid ladder stays best (highest) first; a note under the panel states the derivation and links the official page it comes from. Regression: scripts/tests/test_liquidity_ladder.js drives the shipped page in jsdom against the committed book and asserts the first row is the true best ask with its count, that no raw NO-bid price above 0.50 is printed as an ask, and that the ladder ascends. Mutation-checked: reverting the derivation makes the suite fail with 6 problems, restoring it passes. Wired into scripts/verify_release.py.

flagged.item: Alert topic scope was correct but the page never said WHICH topic rule it enforces; a naive reading of the withheld count looks like 23 swngs are being shown under the wrong topic
flagged.why: Audited on the 2026-11-27T17:15:51Z snapshot: 154 swings are served and 20 archived swings are withheld as out of scope. Of the served rows, 23 belong to series whose official categories are not the topic's name - KXAAAGASCD* (Alaska/California/... retail gas) is filed under Economics, KXAPRPOTUS (Trump approval rating) under Politics, KXPGARYDER and KXPGASOLHEIM (Ryder Cup, Solheim Cup) under Sports. The site's published compatibility rule admits all of those (gas <- Economics, elections <- Politics, golf <- Sports), so nothing is mis-filed: recomputing the rule from the snapshot's own counts.category_compatible_official gives zero contradictions, and the collector's own tag-domain rule (F-97) also passes them. The finding is about auditability, not a wrong number: the page published a bare count ('20 archived swings withheld') without naming the rule or the reason keys, so a reader could not reproduce it. This audit entry records that the 23 rows were checked by hand against GET /series and are correct, and that the check is now automated.
flagged.action: Pinned by scripts/tests/test_alert_topic_domain.js (wired into the release gate): it recomputes the topic rule from counts.category_compatible_official, asserts no served swing contradicts its topic, asserts the published withheld count covers every row absent from the served feed, and asserts every contradicting official category appears in the reasons. No data was changed - the pipeline (scripts/build_alerts.py publishable()) was already applying the rule correctly.

flagged.item: The browser's live path had to infer a market's series from its ticker, and that inference was not exposed or tested; the series-derived fee multiplier and the series-derived topic both depend on it
flagged.why: data/verified_facts.json C-45 records the measured behaviour: GET /markets on the demo environment returns event_ticker but no series_ticker key at all, so the collector derives the series from the ticker prefix and keeps the raw value as series_ticker_from_api. The engine's normalizeRow() does the same thing (assets/engine.js), and the per-series fee multiplier (KXETHY and KXBTCY are maker 0 / taker 0 in the official fee schedule, KXAAAGASM is 1/1) and the live topic classification both read from it. Until this session the derivation was correct but private, so no test could fail if it were changed or deleted - a silent fee error on a live fill would have been invisible to the release gate. Confirmed live on 2026-11-27: GET /markets?status=open&limit=2 returns rows with event_ticker and no series_ticker.
flagged.action: normalizeRow is now exported from assets/engine.js for auditing, and scripts/tests/test_series_fallback.js (wired into the gate) asserts the derivation (KXETHY and KXAAAGASM from the ticker), that a provided series_ticker is never overwritten, that KXETHY resolves to taker multiplier 0 and a 100-contract KXETHY fill therefore costs $0, and that KXAAAGASM at 50c costs the fee schedule's own $1.75. No behaviour was changed; the tolerance in the test is the official schedule's table.

flagged.item: The release gate proved every page RENDERED but never proved a printed number equalled the data; added an independent recomputation of every published figure
flagged.why: scripts/tests/test_pages_dom.js and scripts/tests/test_chatdock.js render all 21 pages in jsdom and check for uncaught errors, leaked placeholder values (missing-value markers rendered as text) and stale wording. None of them compares a rendered value with data/live/*.json, so a page that printed a stale, rounded or hand-typed number would have passed the gate. The brief's verification rule is that every row is source-checked, which needs the arithmetic checked, not just the absence of crashes.
flagged.action: scripts/tests/audit_rendered_numbers.js added and wired into scripts/verify_release.py. It re-derives, with its own arithmetic and without calling assets/*.js: the five landing KPIs and the two disclosure KPIs; the per-topic pick on the landing table (traded rows only, else nearest close_time, labelled untraded) with its dollars, price, contracts and open interest; the 25-row resolution tracker including the literal result of each market; the five category pages' four KPIs, row counts and every row's official source link; the dashboard's five topic cards and their top-8 ranking row by row; the alerts page's two chats (154 swings >= $0.10 verified from to_price - from_price, 123 frozen model picks, the rendered message counts) and the self-consistency of the served ledger; and that all 85 flagged irregularities and 72 verified claims carry a source link. Result on the 2026-11-27T17:15:51Z snapshot: PASS, no discrepancy found in any published figure.

flagged.item: The executive summary's living requirements table typed a volatile count — "the sample is one settled alert" (true on 2026-11-22) — while the alert chats page, rendering the same committed data, showed "settled: 0 … move vs outcome: no settled alert yet"
flagged.why: The number of alerted markets with a finalized yes/no result changes every time the collector's ranked snapshot window rotates: a settled market leaves the 200-row settled window and reads "not in snapshot" (D-03), and new alerts arrive. On the snapshot collected 2026-11-27T17:15:51Z the served feed covers 43 distinct tickers — 15 still open, 28 not in snapshot, 0 settled — so the typed "one settled alert" contradicted the page that actually computes the count. This is the same defect class as F-73 (typed cadence) and D-01 (typed ledger counts): a typed copy of a dynamic value drifts. Verified by rendering alerts.html in jsdom against the committed data (lifecycle bar: "alerted markets: 43, settled: 0, resolved YES: 0, resolved NO: 0, still open: 15, not in snapshot: 28, move vs outcome: no settled alert yet") and by recomputing the join independently from data/live/alerts.json + data/live/markets.json with the same narrow rule assets/site.js uses (finalized status + yes/no result).
flagged.action: Fixed in executive-summary.html: the sentence no longer types a sample size. It keeps the D-04 design disclosure (the move-agrees-with-outcome figure is a bare count, never a rate, because the settled sample is small and changes as markets resolve) and points at the alert chats page, which renders the current count live from the committed snapshot. Pinned by a data-driven regression in scripts/tests/test_pages_dom.js section M: it recomputes the settled-alert sample from the committed alerts + markets with the page's own join and refuses any typed "N settled alert" that disagrees, and requires the bare-count disclosure to remain. Mutation-checked: with the old sentence restored the suite fails ("types a settled-alert sample of 1 but the committed data has 0"); with the fix it passes (0 typed sample sizes). The historical D-04 ledger entry is unchanged — it is the append-only record of what was true when it was written.

flagged.item: The two alert chats and the chat dock counted rows they were not showing: the header said "154 in view" while the feed held 120
flagged.why: The chat header chip on alerts.html printed the size of the whole qualifying set (shownAll.length), while the feed itself was rendered from shownAll.slice(-120). Once the append-only swing archive grew past 120 in-scope rows, the two numbers diverged and the page did not say so. Measured on the committed feed collected 2026-11-27T17:15Z: data/live/alerts.json reports counts.all_events = 154 and counts.high_roi = 123; the all-events chip read "154 in view" and the model chip read "123 in view", but the DOM held 120 and 120 rows respectively - so 34 alerts and 3 model picks were unreachable with nothing on the page disclosing it. The always-on dock on every page had the same defect with its own cap: kdCountAll read "154" while kdChatAll rendered 80 rows, and kdCountModel read "123" while kdChatModel rendered 80. This is the class of defect the project already refuses elsewhere - F-37 and F-90 (a stored count labelled as a found count), F-83 and F-94 (a row presented as the largest when the data does not support it), S-02 (two pages labelling the trimmed count as the found count). For a trader the count next to a chat is a claim about what they have seen; a count larger than the list makes the reader believe they have seen every swing in the archive when they have not.
flagged.action: Fixed. Numbered F-105: the F-100 id was taken by a concurrent session's liquidity-ladder finding (PR #138, now on main) and F-104 by another session's executive-summary stale-count fix (PR #139), so this one takes the next free id. The chip now states what the feed holds, in one of three honest shapes: "N in view" when nothing is held back, "N newest of M" when the render cap is biting, and "N of M qualify" when the traded-only filter is hiding rows. The cap itself stays, because the archive grows without bound and the page must stay responsive, but each chat now carries a control that opens the rows the cap holds back ("Show 34 older alerts"), and once expanded the chip states the full count. The dock's counters use the same rule ("80 of 154"). The second half of the defect is also closed: the browser's alert feed is a ring buffer capped at FEED_MAX = 400, so once the archive passes 400 in-scope swings the oldest would have been dropped silently; the engine now reports the archive's own in-scope size and alerts.html states how many archived swings are not in this page's copy, naming the committed archive that still holds them. Regression: scripts/tests/test_chat_counts.js (mutation-checked - it fails on the pre-fix tree with "the all-events chip states 154 shown and the feed holds 120 rows" and passes after).
